Question: At one of George Washington’s parties, each man shook hands with everyone except his spouse, and no handshakes took place between women. If \(13\) married couples attended, how many handshakes were there among these \(26\) people?
Solution:
Method 1: Method 1: Separate the two handshake types

There are \(13\) men and \(13\) women. Since no two women shake hands, every handshake is either between two men or between a man and a woman who is not his spouse.

Every pair of men shakes hands. Choosing an unordered pair gives
\[
\binom{13}{2}=\frac{13\cdot12}{2}=78.
\]
The division by two accounts for the fact that choosing the same two men in reverse order describes the same handshake.

Each man also shakes hands with \(12\) women, excluding his spouse. This gives \(13\cdot12=156\) handshakes, each counted once by its male participant.

These two types are disjoint and include every permitted handshake. Their total is
\[
78+156=234,
\]
choice \(\mathrm{C}\).

Method 2: Method 2: Count the participants in every handshake

Count one participation whenever one person takes part in one handshake. Each of the \(13\) men shakes hands with \(12\) other men and \(12\) women other than his spouse, giving \(24\) participations per man.

Each of the \(13\) women shakes hands with the \(12\) men other than her spouse and with no women. Thus the total number of participations is
\[
13\cdot24+13\cdot12=468.
\]
Every handshake contributes exactly two participations, one from each person. Dividing by two therefore counts every handshake exactly once:
\[
\frac{468}{2}=234.
\]
There are \(234\) handshakes, choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
